  SUBJECT:  Consideration of Tyler Technologies, lnc.'s request for substantive
  changes to agreement for Enterprise Resource Planning Software
  System (awarded December 5, 2018)

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Authorizing the City Manager to execute a contract (awarded December 5,
  2018), in a form approved by the City Attorney, including substantive changes
  requested by Tyler Technologies, lnc. for the purchase, installation, licensing
  and maintenance of an Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) Software
  System; and

  2. Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXEGUTIVE SUMMARY:

On December 5, 2018, the City Council awarded a contract for an ERP software system
to Tyler Technologies, lnc. ("Tyler"). Since that time, staff worked with Tyler to fine-tune
the contract language including, without limitation, material terms and conditions that
Tyler identified as being important in its July 2018 proposal. Most of these are now
resolved and included several additional concessions by Tyler. There are three areas,
however, that require City Council consideration and approval: limitation of liability;
insurance; and indemnification language. Based upon the concessions supplied by
Tyler - and its status within the industry - staff believes that it is in the public interest for
the City Council to accept Tyler's proposed language.

BACKGROUND:

An overview of the City's need for an ERP software system, the RFP process, and the
reasons that Tyler was selected as the successful vendor are explained in the attached
staff report from December 5, 2018. Based upon that Staff Report, staffs
recommendation, and Tyler's presentation during the Council meeting, the City Council
voted to award Tyler the contract.

  Page 6 of 406
 Tyler Technologies Staff Report
March 13,2019
Page2

The Staff Report did not explicitly identify exceptions noted by Tyler via letter dated July
23,2018 which accompanied its proposal. A copy of that letter is attached for reference
(the "Tyler Letter"). Staff believed that these items could be resolved with Tyler before
the contract was executed pursuant to Council's direction. That belief was mostly
correct. Three items, however, cannot be determined at an administrative level: Tyler's
requested changes to (1) the City's standard indemnification clause; (2) the City's
standard insurance requirements; and (3) Tyler's desire for a limitation of liability.
Resolution No. 1 1750 explicitly requires Council approval for changes to the insurance.
As to the indemnification and the limitation of liability, the City Council should be the one
determining whether the concessions offered by Tyler during the negotiations process
(i.e., since December 2018) are sufficient to outweigh the potential risks resulting from
the changes proposed by Tyler.

Technology companies frequently include a limitation on liability clause in their
agreements. Historically, the City has been moderately successful in either removing
the clauses altogether or, at a minimum, increasing the liability cap. lf the clauses
remain, the City seeks to match the cap with the insurance policy limit required for a
contract (e.9., $ZM which is the City's standard insurance requirement).

Tyler's request provides for a cap on liability that equates to approximately $590K; the
City sought to remove the clause or, at least, equate the cap to the insurance
requirements ($2M). While Tyler rejected that proposal, it is willing to double the cap to
approximately $1.2M.

Since the overall contract is valued at approximately $900,000, the decision regarding
this clause must be made by the City Council.

On June 17,2015, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 11750 which establishes
the City's insurance requirements for all agreements (as defined in the Resolution).
Section a(D) of the Resolution requires City Council approval for any change in
insurance requirements where the City Attorney opines a contract has high risk. The
ERP contemplated by this contract affects all City financial transactions; the software
tracks virtually every aspect of the City's revenue and expenditures. Additionally, the
contract contemplates training at City Hall by vendor employees; travel; and other risk
factors. Consequently, the City Attorney views this contract as "high risk" (based on
Section 9 of Resolution No. 11750).

Tyler proposes insurance that differs from the City's insurance requirements (and what
was set forth in the RFP). Here are the specific differences:

  1. City requires a Best AM Rating of "A:Vll." Tyler is offering "A-:Vll."

  Page 7 of 406
 Tyler Technologies Staff Report
March 13,2019
Page 3

  2. City requires $2M per occurrence; Tyler is offering $2M in aggregate (though it
  also is providing a $5M umbrella policy, per occurrence, and a $5M umbrella
  policy, in aggregate, that should offset the City's risk).

  3. City reserves the ability to review deductibles; Tyler does not want the City to
  approve the deductible amounts but did provide the range of deductibles (see its
  attached response).

  4. City wishes to have the option of reviewing the insurance policy (as an additional
  insured); Tyler (per the Tyler Letter and its February 1"t response) considers such
  policies confidential.

Tyler's position is that its

  "insurance is established at the corporate level. Tyler is not willing to
  change the way it insures its entire corporation upon individual client
  requests. The changes to the City's language here reflect the reality of
  Tyler's current insurance program. Tyler carries more than adequate
  levels of insurance, and these insurance levels have been accepted by
  dozens of California municipalities."

Staff is informed by the City Attorney's office that the City's risk in accepting these
proposed changes is likely low:

  1. The difference in AM Best rating is negligible: both an "4" and an "A-" rating is
  considered "excellent" which equates to a company having "a superior ability to
  meet [its] ongoing obligations to policyholders."

  2. While $2M per occurrence is preferred, the two $5M umbrella policies should
  provide sufficient insurance to the City in the event of an unforeseen event.

  3. Tyler shared that its current SIR is $10,000 for Umbrella Liability; current
  deductibles are $1,000 for Auto and $500,000 for Professional Liability. These
  seem to be reasonable sums for the City to pay in the event Tyler cannot.

  4. lt is likely that the insurance policy information is not required on the front-end of
  the contract so long as the City is added as an additional insured to that policy.
  One option might be to require Tyler to place its insurance policy into an escrow
  that could be accessed by the City in the event of a claim.

Based upon these factors, staff recommends that the City Council accept Tyler's
proposal.

  Page 8 of 406
 Tyler Technologies Staff Report
March 13,2019
Page 4

Tyler's proposed indemnification language differs from the City's standard clauses. The
City's contract templates use a bifurcated indemnification clause to ensure that the City
is protected from professional negligence, willful acts, other negligence, and violations
of applicable law. The clause related to professional negligence is covered by
professional liability insurance; the "general" clause for general damages is insured via
commercial general liability (or "CGL") insurance. Professional liability insurance does
not provide a defense to the City, i.e., it does not provide an actual attorney, but does
reimburse for defense costs. CGL, however, provides a defense (and pays for it).

The City's "general" indemnification clause provides very broad protection to the City; it
transfers the maximum risk permissible from the City to the vendor. lt also gives the City
a reasonable ability to choose its defense counsel. The latter is important since there
may be instances where the City would choose to select its own defense counsel in a
lawsuit (for various reasons) but be reimbursed for defense costs.

To help with its own risk management, Tyler seeks to narrow the City's indemnification
language. Among other things, Tyler proposes language that would allow it to solely
control the defense (and defense counsel) of any litigation (with the City's cooperation)
and increases the City's potential exposure to liability, i.e., the City might - under some
circumstances - be required to contribute to settlements or judgments. ln its statement
dated February 1,2019, Tyler noted that it is open to discussing the types of claims
about which the City may be concerned.

It is difficult to fully identify all the risks that are involved with this agreement. The ERP
software will control all City financial records. Risks for this include, without limitation, a
system-wide shutdown that would interfere with payroll, vendor payments, retirement,
etc.; miscalculations as to permit fees, refunds, taxes, retirement, etc.; software glitches
or malware that would affect the rest of the City's network; or personal injury and/or
property damage resulting from e.9., Tyler employees traveling/to from City Hall for
training sessions. The list goes on. Because of this uncertainty, it seems desirable to
implement the City's general policy: transfer as much risk as possible to the vendor.
Alternatively, the City Council's direction to the City Attorney could be to negotiate the
indemnification language to the mutual satisfaction of both parties while still ensuring
the City was protected to the greatest extent practicable.

ln light of Tyler's requests regarding a limitation on liability, insurance, and
indemnification, staff sought additional concessions from Tyler to off-set the potential
risks. On March 1, 2019, Tyler offered the following:

  a  Tyler will maintain its 2016 prices for this contract. As a result, the City benefits

  will be high quality. The building finishes include smooth stucco in various earth tones,

  design will be consistent with the architectural styles that the Planning Commission has

  Square, the existing commercial buildings along Atlantic Boulevard, between West

  architectural styles were reflective of that time period. Within the past five years, the
  Planning Commission has approved the Courtyard by Marriott, Hilton Doubletree, and
  the AG Hotel, which all have contemporary/modern styles.

B.  The proposed buildings or structures are not of inferior quality such as to cause the
  nature of the local environment to materially depreciate in appearance and value.

  project will provide new street trees along Atlantic Boulevard as well as throughout the
  project in raised planters. According to MPMC S 21.14.090(C), a 12 feet wide
  pedestrian realm is required on Atlantic Boulevard and a 13 feet wide pedestrian realm

  DATE: March 20,2019

TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
FROM:  Vincent D. Chang, City Clerk
SUBJECT:  Public Hearing to Receive lnput from the Community Regarding the
  Creation of a City Council District-Based Electoral System Pursuant to
  Elections Code 510010

RECOMMENDATION:

  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Conducting a Public Hearing to receive public testimony on the composition
  of districts for a district-based electoral system pursuant to Elections Code
  s 10010;
  (2) Providing direction to the City's demographer regarding the composition of
  districts for a district-based electoral system pursuant to Elections Code $
  10010; and
  (3) Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXEGUTIVE SUMMARY:

On November 7, 2018, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 12043 declaring its
intent to transition from at-large to district-based elections for City Council commencing
with the General Municipal Election in March 2020. Elections Code S 10010 requires
that the City conduct four public hearings to receive community input on district
boundaries and maps for the formation of City Council districts.

On December 19, 2018, the City Council conducted the second of four Public Hearings.
Community input regarding the composition of district boundaries is summarized in
Attachment 1.

Based on public input, the City Council's direction, and other legally required criteria, the
City's Demographer evaluated and submitted the proposed draft maps for public review
and comments. lt is recommended that the City Council give direction regarding which
final map product, with any necessary modifications, the City Council would like to
consider at the March 6th City Council Meeting.

BACKGROUND

Since November 7th, the City engaged in outreach efforts to inform the public about
district elections and the process associated with their formation. A webpage
(www.MontereyPark.ca.gov/DistrictElections) was uploaded to provide information
about district elections, including opportunities for when and how the public can be
engaged (translations available). The official notice of Public Hearings was translated
and published in the Monterey Park Press (English), La Opinión (Spanish), World
Journal (Chinese), and Saigon Times (Vietnamese). ln addition, a press release in
multiple languages was sent via email to local media and subscribers, and an article
was placed in the December 2018 and the February 2019 editions of the Monterey Park
Cascade which was mailed to every residence in the City.

At the December 19, 2018 council meeting, the City Council directed staff to conduct
additional outreach efforts to engage the community in the formation of city council
districts. On the week of Jan. 14, 2019, a postcard, in multiple languages, providing
notice of the formation of district based electoral system was mailed to each household
in the City. The announcement was also emailed to City's Commissions and Board
members. Additional, public participation kits were made available throughout city hall
and an instructional video on how to use the participation tools was uploaded to the
webpage as well. Persons calling for more information and request for the kit were
mailed a public participation kit.

At the February 20, 2019 council meeting, the City Council continued the previously
scheduled March 6, 2019 Public Hearing to March 20, 2019 and set the deadline of
March 8, 2019 4:30 p.m. as the deadline for submittal of 5 districts maps. By
consensus, the City Council eliminated Maps Nos. 1,2,6,7,8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15,
and 16, for reasons including over or under 5 districts, population imbalance or may
have protected class dilution or other challenges. The City Council moved forward for
consideration at the next meeting Maps Nos. 3, 4, 5, 9, 17, and 18.

Leading up to the fourth public hearing, the City Clerk's office received multiple
proposed draft maps. These maps were evaluated by the City's Demographer and are
confirmed that they have met the standards established under the California Voting
Right Act (CVRA) and Federal Voting Rights Act (FVRA). Attachment 2 includes newly
proposed maps and maps carried over from the last meeting for review and public
comments.

Elections Code S 10010 requires that modifications to the boundary maps be
republished for public review at least seven days before City Council consideration. lt is
recommended that the Cíty Council give direction regarding which final map product,
with any necessary modifications, for consideration and adoption at the April 3, 2019.

Next Steps

At the April 3, 2019 City Council Meeting, the City Council will conduct a Sth Public
Hearing to adopt a preferred district map and to introduce an ordinance to transition to a
district-based electoral system. The ordinance would take effect 30 days after its
adoption and will govern the 2020 general municipal elections.

allocated $50,000 and $10,000, respectively, for costs associated with district voting.

New comments:
Lee 1 – submitted by Chai Lee
  I personally don't think this makes sense for a small city like ours, maybe for a city with
  millions of residents. Seeing that it is the law we have no choice, hopefully this map will
  meet all the legal requirements.
Dem 2 – submitted by Monterey Park Democratic Club
  We wanted districts that are compact, that had a community of interest, and which have a
  blend of homes and commerce. - Craig Athon (MPDC Secretary)
Lister 3 – submitted by Jason Lister
  I think this map makes sense because the districts are compact, and the boundaries roughly
  follow topography and natural dividing lines. It attempts to group together similar
  neighborhoods, and similar communities of interest so that they have representation.
  Census tracts should be divided up (adjustments to the district boundaries made) to make
  the districts more population balanced. It is suggested to allow candidates living outside of
  the district to run provided the candidate lives in Monterey Park.

Previous map comments:
Dhing 1 – submitted by Jason Dhing
  The following criterias are used to create the 5 districts:
  1  District 3 is created first based on the highest Hispanic percentage of total
  population. The Unit ID numbers that have percentage of population of Hispanics 35% or
  more are circled in the colored Population Unit ID Map (attached with email).
  2  Approximate elementary school boundaries (based on Population Unit ID) of each
  Alhambra Unified School District are next drawn on the map as guidelines for the other 4
  districts.
  3  Each Population Unit ID are added to each based on the first 2 criteria, with a
  conscious balance of Number of Population, Voters and Registration in mind. Each district
  has almost equal number of Population, equal number of Voters and equal number of
  Registration.
  4  Population Unit ID# 22 and 1 are purposely left out, because ID#22 is East Los
  Angeles College, and ID#1 is Monterey Park Marketplace. These two IDs should never be
  controlled by any district. Each district has some share of each of the business districts of
  the city [NDC note: Population Units 22 and 1 have been added to their surrounding districts by NDC
  because by law all city territory must be assigned to a district.]

Dhing 1 – submitted by Jason Dhing
  The following criterias are used to create the 5 districts:
  1  District 3 is created first based on the highest Hispanic percentage of total
  population. The Unit ID numbers that have percentage of population of Hispanics 35% or
  more are circled in the colored Population Unit ID Map (attached with email).
  2  Approximate elementary school boundaries (based on Population Unit ID) of each
  Alhambra Unified School District are next drawn on the map as guidelines for the other 4
  districts.
  3  Each Population Unit ID are added to each based on the first 2 criteria, with a
  conscious balance of Number of Population, Voters and Registration in mind. Each district
  has almost equal number of Population, equal number of Voters and equal number of
  Registration.
  4  Population Unit ID# 22 and 1 are purposely left out, because ID#22 is East Los
  Angeles College, and ID#1 is Monterey Park Marketplace. These two IDs should never be
  controlled by any district. Each district has some share of each of the business districts of
  the city [NDC note: Population Units 22 and 1 have been added to their surrounding districts by NDC
  because by law all city territory must be assigned to a district.]

Lau 1 – submitted by Gary Lau
  I think this map makes sense because first and foremost it takes into consideration the racial
  makeup of the areas. Secondly, business interest for the main thoroughfares of Garfield,
  Atlantic, & Garvey is concentrated under 2 districts only. Thirdly, this map provides a
  sensible separation between commercial and residential interest. In summary, I think this
  approach offers a fair and logical political representation for the city's residents and
  businesses.
Lau 1, 2, 3 and 4 – submitted by Bill Lam
  Districts based on “attendance zones for school, parks, and some communities.”
Yee 1 – submitted by Cindy Yee
  Comments in separate letter from Ms. Yee.
Fromdatower 1 – Submitted by Teki Fromdatower

Lopez 1 – Submitted by Mike Lopez
  I think this map makes sense because: it follows the boundaries of most school districts and
  school communities, keeps neighborhoods together, reduces confusion (because current
  council members are each represented in a separate district) and a Latino district of 56% is
  created as required by the California Voting Rights Act.

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting a Resolution providing notice of an intent to amend the City's CaIPERS
  contract to increase contributions made by FFA members to CaIPERS retirement
  costs;
  2. Waive first reading and introduce an Ordinance that would amend the City's
  CaIPERS contract. Second reading and adoption would be scheduled for April 3,
  2019;

  Code Section 7507'; and
  4. Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

Ïhe 201 8-2022 Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the City and Monterey
Park Firefighters' Association includes an agreement that the City amend the CaIPERS
contract to increase the contribution by FFA members toward retirement costs. That
amendment would result in FFA members increasing their own contributions as follows:
a 3% increase for classic employees and 0.5% for new employees. lncluded in the
MOU is a provision that FFA classic and FFA PEPRA members pay a share of PERS
for a total contribution of 12o/o.

BACKGROUND:

On November 7, 2018, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 12047 which approved
the MOU with FFA for contract year 2018-2022. Among other things, the MOU provides
that the City and FFA will amend the terms of 1) Article 21-Retirement Benefits and 2)

Department to utilize special assignments in a particular beat due to identifiable crime trends.

Spirit Bus Program Overview

The City of Monterey Park established the fixed-route transit system called Spirit Bus in
1989. Currently, there are five routes that serve different areas of the City. Route I & 3
and 2 & 4 run the same fixed route in the City during the same hours but in opposite
directions. Route 5 connects the Metrolink Station at Cal State LA campus, East Los
Angeles College, and the McCaslin Business Park. ln addition, the City operates the
Metrolink shuttle (part of Route 5) during the morning and afternoon peak hours
connecting the Metrolink stop at Cal State LA campus and East Los Angeles College.

There are 36 stops along each route except for Route 5 there are 20 stops. The hours
of the program are Monday through Friday from 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. and Saturdays
from 9:10 a.m. to 5:45 p.m. The fixed-route buses do not operate on Sunday. The cost
to ride the fixed-route system is $0.25 per trip for Routes 1 - 4 and $0.50 for Route 5
and Metrolink shuttle. This price was set in early 1990s and remains the same since
then. The fare includes one free transfer to other Spirit Bus lines and Metro buses within
the first 1.5 hours.

There is one 2O-passenger bus and five 3O-passenger buses in the City's inventory to
operate this program with additional three new buses coming onboard very soon. The
buses generally have a 7-year life span; current vehicles were purchased in 2011,2012,
2013,2015, and 2018. Since the buses operate on a hillside, they require more
maintenance than other vehicles. The 201 1 and 2012 vehides are approaching the end
of its lifespan and coming due for replacement. All of the fixed-route vehicles are
powered by Compressed Natural Gas (CNG). The cost to replace vehicles of this size
and capacity cost approximately $250,000-$300,000.

Proposed Changes to the City's Transit System

Option 1: lssue RFP to Continue the Fixed-Route Service

The RFP is attached in this staff report for the City Council's approval and direction. The
RFP will be sent to as many transit service contractors as possible. Note that under this
option the biggest challenge for transportation service contractors is maintaining a
reliable fleet of buses. The City already contracted with a few contractors, including MV
Transportation, First Transit, and Transportation Concepts. First Transit is currently
operating the Spirit Bus from July 2015 to present; MV Transportation operated the
Spirit Bus from July 2010 to June 2015; First Transit had the contract before MV
Transportation from July 2004 to June 2010; and Transportation Concepts before First
Transit from July 2001 to June 2004. All these contractors previously experienced
similar issues, such as high management staff turnover rate, poor performance related
to vehicle maintenance, and poor customer service level.

To ensure that the contractor is accountable to performance standards, strict liquidated
damages were included to the proposed Spirit Bus Agreement. The intent of the
liquidated damages is to reimburse the City for damages resulting from the contractor

PROPOSED TRANSPORTATION SERVICES

Monterey Park was incorporated in 1916. Totaling7.73 square miles in size, Monterey
Park is home to more than 60,000 residents and is conveniently located less than 20
minutes from Downtown Los Angeles. Using Proposition A and Proposition C Local Tax
Return Funds, the City of Monterey Park has provided its residents with fixed-route
service, Spirit Bus, since 1989. Monterey Park has consistently ranked as one of the
country's best places to live due to its good schools, growing economy, and central
location.

The City provides fixed route transit service designed to provide transportation for
residents within the community The selected Contractor must provide everything
necessary to operate this service, including, but not limited to: all labor, equipment, tools,
fuel, materials and supplies, insurance, supervision, and all other items needed to deliver
exceptional, on-time transportation services. Furthermore, the Contractor will be
responsible for all data collection efforts. The Contractor will recommend operating hours
and policies, routes, and fares; the City will make the final determination for operating
hours and policies, routes, and fares. The City will also be responsible for marketing the
services, the Contractor must cooperate with marketing efforts, surveys, etc.

The City of Monterey Park emphasizes courtesy to passengers and on{ime performance,
as well as clean, well-maintained, accessible, and mechanically safe vehicles. All transit
services must meet City, State, and Federal standards, including, but not limited to, all
transit and air quality regulations, as well as compliance with the provisions of the
Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

The City will establish a system of controls and standards with the Contractor to ensure
compliance with the performance and service standards for this operation. lt is the City's
intention to meet the following objectives through this award of contract. All requirements
provided in this RFP are aimed at addressing these goals:

  A.  Maintain a strong commitment to providing customer satisfaction through
  friendly and courteous service;
  B.  Establish a safe and reliable service that meets or exceeds the service and
  performance standards as defined in this RFP;
  C.  Establish a long-term, stable relationship with a provider who can bring
  efficiencies, new methods, new technology and techniques to implement a
  successful transit service; and
  D.  Provide a cost-effective service to maximize available resources.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE
  CITY OF MONTEREY PARK, CALIFORNIA
  DECLARING THE MONTH OF MARCH AS WOMEN'S
  HISTORY MONTH, A NATIONAL CELEBRATION
  THAT HIGHLIGHTS THE CONTRIBUTIONS OF
  WOMEN TO EVENTS IN HISTORY AND
  CONTEMPORARY SOCIETY

The City Council of the City of Monterey Park does resolve as follows

SECTION  1. The City Council finds and declares that:
  A. ln February 1980, President Jimmy Carter issued a presidential proclamation
  declaring the week of March B, 1980, as National Women's Week. The
  proclamation stated, "From the first settlers who came to our shores, from the first
  American lndian families who befriended them, men and women have worked
  together to build this nation. Too often the women were unsung and sometimes
  their contributions went unnoticed. However, the achievements, leadership,
  courage, strength and love of the women who built America were as vital as that of
  the men whose names we know so well."

  B. Women's History Month originated as a national celebration in 1981 when
  Congress passed Public Law 97-28 which authorized and requested the President
  Reagan to proclaim the week beginning March 7, 1982 as "Women's History
  Week."

  C. Throughout the next five years, Congress continued to pass joint resolutions
  designating a week in March as "Women's History Week."

  D. Maryland, Alaska, Pennsylvania, New York, Oregon, and other states developed
  and distributed curriculum materials in all of their public schools, which prompted
  educational events such as essay contests. Within a few years, thousands of
  schools and communities introduced and celebrated National Women's History
  Week, supported and encouraged by resolutions from governors, city councils,
  school boards, and the U.S. Congress.

  E. By 1986, fourteen states had already declared March as Women's History Month
  F. ln 1987 after being petitioned by the NationalWomen's History Project, Congress
  passed Public Law 100-9 which designed the month of March 1987 as "Women's
  History Month."

  Page 404 of 406

  G. Between 19BB and 1994, Congress passed additionalresolutions requesting and
  authorizing the President to proclaim March of each year as Women's History
  Month.

  H. Since 1995, Presidents Clinton, Bush, Obama, and Trump have issued a series of
  annual proclamations designating the month of March as "Women's History
  Month."

  "Women's History Month" corresponds with the lnternational Women's Day
  celebrated on March 8th worldwide; it contributes an opportunity to celebrate the
  achievements of women while calling for greater equality.

  J. An example of strong leaders who struggled for equality and should be celebrated
  during the month of March lnclude: Susan B. Anthony, Sojourner Truth, Lucy
  Stone, Lucretia Mott, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Harriet Tubman, and Alice Paul.

  K. American women have played and continue to play a critical economic, cultural,
  and social role in every sphere of the life of the Nation by constituting a significant
  portion of the labor force working inside and outside of the home.

  L. American women have been leaders, not only in securing their own rights of
  suffrage and equal opportunity, but also in the abolitionist movement, the
  emancipation movement, the industrial labor movement, the civil rights movement,
  and other movements, especially the peace movement, which create a more fair
  and just society for all.

  M. American women have created a legacy that continues to inspire generations of
  women to live with confidence, to have a positive impact on their communities, and
  to improve our Nation.

SECTION  2. The City Council further declares:
  A. The month of March as Women's History Month and encourages all residents to
  celebrate lnternational Women's Month during the month of March with
  appropriate programs, ceremonies, and activities.

2A. CONSIDERATION OF TYLER TECHNOLOGIES, INC.'S REQUEST FOR
  SUBSTANTIVE CHANGES TO AGREEMENT FOR ENTERPRISE RESOURCE
  PLANNING SOFTWARE SYSTEM (AWARDED DECEMBER 5, 2018)

  On December 5, 2018, the City Council awarded a contract for an ERP software
  system to Tyler Technologies, lnc. ("Tyler"). Since that time, staff worked with Tyler
  to fine-tune the contract language including, without limitation, material terms and
  conditions that Tyler identified as being important in its July 2018 proposal. Most of
  these are now resolved and included several additional concessions by Tyler.
  There are three areas, however, that require City Council consideration and
  approval: limitation of liability; insurance; and indemnification language. Based
  upon the concessions supplied by Tyler - and its status within the industry - staff
  believes that it is in the public interest for the City Council to accept Tyler's
  proposed language.

  This item was heard after ltem No. 58

  Action Taken: The City Council authorized the City Manager to execute a contract
  (awarded December 5,2018), in a form approved by the City Attorney, including
  substantive changes requested by Tyler Technologies, lnc. for the purchase,
  installation, licensing and maintenance of an Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP)
  Software System as amended to direct staff to continue discussion with Tyler
  Technologies regarding the indemnification and to give authority to the City
  Attorney to approve the contract.

4. PUBLIC HEARING
4A. PUBLIC HEARING TO RECEIVE INPUT FROM THE COMMUNITY REGARDING
  THE CREATION OF A CITY COUNCIL DISTRICT.BASED ELECTORAL
  SYSTEM PURSUANT TO ELECTTONS CODE 510010

  On November 7,2018, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 12043 declaring
  its intent to transition from at-large to district-based elections for City Council
  commencing with the General Municipal Election in March 2020. Elections Code $
  10010 requires that the City conduct four public hearíngs to receive community
  input on district boundaries and maps for the formation of City Council districts.

  On December 19,2018, the City Council conducted the second of four Public
  Hearings. Community input regarding the composition of district boundaries is
  summarized in Attachment 1 of the staff report.

  Based on public input, the City Council's direction, and other legally required
  criteria, the City's Demographer evaluated and submitted the proposed draft maps
  for public review and comments. lt is recommended that the City Council give
  direction regarding which final map product, with any necessary modifications, the
  City Council would like to consider at the March 6th City Council Meeting.
   67- 057
  March 20,2019
 Public Speakers:

- Robert McEntire, City Consultant and representative of the National Demographics
 Corporation (NDC) team, presented a summary and reviewed 18 proposed maps,
 4 of which were from NDC. He was available to answer questions.

- Michael Lopez, said his map is based on school districts boundaries which do not
 break up the community interest based on visible boundaries. He provided an
 example stating that north and south Riggin are both in the same school district
 and are not separated into different districts in his map. He clarified that his
 intention was not to pair Mayor Pro Tem Liang and Council Member lng in the
 same district.

- Bill Lam, stated he had look at othercities with 5, 7 and 9 districts and understands
 that adding additional seats will require voters approval. He said he drew a
 centralize style map with no pairing of council members and one using major
 streets like Garfield and Atlantic as boundaries to match the precinct areas closer
 to polling locations. He stated the southern region should be up for 2020 election.
 He clarified that he did not realize the 2 maps limitation and his Map No. 24 was
 not population balance. He expressed that he would like to see a 5 districts map
 from the South or the United South category, using major streets such as Atlantic,
 Garfield, Garvey or Floral west of Atlantic to split up the districts. He concluded by
 encouraging the district members to work beyond their district boundaries and look
 at other issues.

- David Barron, recommended the council to review the spirit and the intention of
 transitioning to district based electoral system, and to focus on diversify in the
 areas of interests, ethnicity or the council. He encouraged the council to choose a
 map with a potential of selecting two Latino members to serve on the council. He
 said he favored Map 5 which he feels has potential and it does not divide his
 neighbors into two districts. He concluded that he still believes in a 7 district
 council and encouraged the council to place the question out to the voters.

- City Clerk Chang read into the records a written communication received via email
 from Jason Lister with a response from NDC.

 Action Taken: The Mayor opened the Public Hearing at 7:47 p.m. and received
 public testimony and closed the Public Hearing at 8:08 p.m. on the composition of
 districts for a district-based electoral system pursuant to Elections Code S 10010.
 The City Council provided direction to staff to continue the Public Hearing to April
 3,2019, and directed the City's Demographer not to process any additional maps
 submitted.

  TO JUNE 30,2022

  Representatives of the City of Monterey Park have met on numerous occasions
  with representative of the Monterey Park Police Officers' Association (POA)
  regarding wages, CaIPERS cost sharing, deferred compensation contribution,
  Retiree Healthcare Trust (RHT), a one-time cash payment compensation and other
  terms and conditions of employment. The results of these negotiations are
  contained in the attached Memoranda of Understanding (MOU), which is being
  presented to the City Council for approval via adopting an implementíng
  Resolution

  The City and the POA worked through the negotiations process and focused on a
  four-year contract with the bulk of the cost in the last two years of the four-year
  contract. This will be the first four-year contract with POA in the last decade;
  previous contracts have typically been a two-year term.

5C. AUTHORTZATTON TO ADVERTTSE THE REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL (RFP) FOR
  SPIRIT BUS AND CONSIDERAT¡ON OF TRANSIT PROGRAM CHANGE

  The existing fixed-route services Spirit Bus contract with First Transit will expire on
  June 30, 2019. Staff prepared a request for proposal (RFP) for Spirit Bus and
  seeks City Council authorization to advertise the RFP. Staff also recommends that
  the City Council consider the efficacy of the City's fixed-route transit system and
  provide direction on how to proceed with Spirit Bus.

  CEQA (CALTFORNTA ENVTRONMENTAL QUALTTY ACT):
  Taking the recommended action would not result in a potential for resulting in a
  direct or reasonably indirect physical change in the environment and, accordingly,
  does not qualify as a "project" under the California Environmental Quality Act (Cal.
  Pub. Res. Code SS 21000, ef seg.; "CEQA") or CEQA regulations (Cal. Code
  Regs. tit. 14, SS 15000, ef seg.; see Cal. Code Regs. t¡t. 14, SS 15061(bX3),
  15378). Even if the award of contract were to qualify as a project, it would be
  categorically exempt as a Class 1 or Class 5 project since, at best, it would
  constitute a minor alteration of existing public structures involving no expansion of
  use; or a minor alteration in land use limitations (see Cal. Code Regs. tit. 14, S$
  15301,15305).

  Action Taken: The City Council authorized staff to advertise the Request for
  Proposal (RFP) for the City's Fixed-Route Transit Services - Spirit Bus, and
  provided direction to staff regarding the Fixed-Route Transit Services Contract and
  Program by requesting a report be brought back for discussion considering a
  change in bus routes and bus fare, and the Alternatíve Mobility Program.
